title: The Martyrdom of Polycarp
hook: the oldest account of a martyr outside the New Testament
tomorrow: who wrote a whole Sunday service down for an emperor to read?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius writing to his friend Polycarp: stand like an anvil, struck and still standing. The line was an anvil. Today, the friend.

Some insults get flipped. A word thrown at a group becomes the word they throw back. In a stadium in Smyrna, a crowd is chanting at the Christians: away with the atheists. They've arrested the old bishop, Polycarp, and the governor offers him a way out: just say it. Away with the atheists. And Polycarp says it. He looks hard at the packed stands, waves his hand toward the crowd, groans, looks up to heaven, and says: away with the atheists. Why would a bishop say that?
screen: `A WORD THROWN, A WORD THROWN BACK.` → `JUST SAY IT.` → `AND HE SAYS IT.`

segments.voice: First, the flip. In the story, atheists is the crowd's name for the Christians, who won't swear by Caesar or honor the city's gods. Polycarp says the words, but with his hand pointed at the crowd. Same words, opposite aim. Second, the answer. The governor presses: swear, curse Christ, and I'll let you go. Polycarp answers, in the old Schaff translation: "Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury." How could he curse his King, who saved him? Third, the fire. Threatened with fire, he says theirs burns for an hour and goes out. When it's lit, the letter says, the flames arch around him like a ship's sail filled with wind, and he is like bread baking. The story ends with his death, told plainly and without cruelty. Fourth, the letter itself. His church in Smyrna wrote all of it down and sent it to another church, and to the communities of the holy and catholic Church in every place, asking them to pass it on. Some readers call it the oldest martyr story we have outside the New Testament. His friends gathered his bones as more precious than jewels, and planned to keep the day he died as a birthday.
screen: `THE SAME WORDS, AIMED AT THE CROWD.` · `HE NEVER DID ME ANY INJURY.` · `FLAMES LIKE A SAIL.` · `A LETTER FOR EVERY CHURCH.` · then, large: `THE OLDEST STORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where people are hurt or threatened for what they believe, whatever their faith. Say its name out loud, slowly, once every few breaths. Polycarp's church wrote so faraway strangers would remember; if you pray, let each name be a prayer for them.
The Martyrdom of Polycarp. A letter from his own church: an old bishop who would not curse the King he had served.
Pocket this one: the oldest story, written down so the next church would hear it too. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Polycarp's feast each year and name martyrs in their prayers; many parishes also pray in the intercessions for people persecuted for their faith.

fork.setup: your teammate's family offers her a paid summer trip if she stops going to Mass. she's served at that parish for years. what's Polycarp's kind of answer?
options: a kind no: what she's served for years has never done her wrong.
take the trip now and quietly go back to Mass afterward.
say yes; old loyalties shouldn't cost anybody a summer.
fork.reveal: offered his freedom for one sentence, Polycarp answered from his whole life: he had served Christ for years and never been wronged. how could he curse his King?

original.note: Greek for a witness or testimony: the word this letter's title is built on.

trapdoor: what you thought: a martyr story is mostly about how someone died.
what it means: a witness. Polycarp's whole life of serving Christ, said in one sentence to the governor.
what a scholar hears: a church's letter, greeting the holy and catholic Church in every place and asking to be passed on.
guess: a letter telling how Polycarp died as a witness
a sermon Polycarp preached before his arrest
the rule Polycarp wrote for his church in Smyrna
recall: his letter: let me be God's wheat

chat.says: abuela moves in saturday. at dinner she prayed for people hurt for their faith overseas. why strangers?
options: Polycarp's church wrote his story so far-off churches would remember. Praying for strangers keeps that going.
She's being polite. Grace before dinner is really meant for the people sitting at the table.
Mostly for her own church's people. Martyr stories are about remembering your own side.
chat.meaning: Smyrna sent Polycarp's story to churches everywhere and asked them to pass it on. Remembering strangers who suffer is part of how the story lives.

Polycarp.meaning: bishop of Smyrna, Ignatius's friend, put to death for his faith

Smyrna.meaning: the city where Polycarp was bishop and died

Martyrdom.meaning: dying as a witness to one's faith

catholic.meaning: here: the whole Church, in every place

notes: Confirm the Martyrdom of Polycarp 9 wording against Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Schaff edition, Roberts and Donaldson). The count 'eighty and six years' is in the cited text.

Paraphrased: the crowd's cry 'away with the atheists' (ch. 3); the proconsul telling him to swear by the fortune of Caesar and say 'away with the atheists', and Polycarp looking at the crowd, waving his hand toward them, groaning and looking up to heaven (ch. 9); the fire that burns for an hour (ch. 11); the flames like a ship's sail and 'like bread that is baked' (ch. 15); bones 'more precious than jewels' and the birthday of his martyrdom (ch. 18); the greeting to the church at Philomelium and all the communities of the holy and catholic Church in every place, and the request to pass the letter on (greeting, ch. 20).

The index hook calls it the oldest account of a martyr outside the New Testament; under the claims rule the script says 'some readers call it' and the carry is kept exactly. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable.
'Who won't swear by Caesar or honor the city's gods' explains 'atheists' from the story's own context (the oath by Caesar's fortune); confirm wording.

For parents: the lesson includes Polycarp's death by fire and sword; the script names the fire only through the letter's sail-and-bread image and says his death is told plainly, with no graphic detail.
The practice invites naming any place where people are hurt for their faith, of any tradition.
